title: LLM Inference Optimization (vLLM, TGI)
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# LLM Inference Optimization (vLLM, TGI) ##### 4 requests per second on an A100 A team in Pune served a fine-tuned Llama-3-8B behind a FastAPI endpoint. The handler was a straightforward Hugging Face `generate()` call, one request at a time. On an A100 costing ₹250 an hour they achieved **4 requests per second**. At their traffic they needed 60. Six A100s, ₹1,500 an hour, ₹1.1 crore a year. They switched to vLLM. Same model, same hardware, same outputs. **71 requests per second on one GPU.** An 18× improvement with no model change. The gain came from three things their naive loop was throwing away: requests were processed sequentially instead of batched, the KV cache was pre-allocated to the maximum sequence length so most of it sat empty, and every request waited for the slowest one in its batch to finish. **Inference optimisation is where the largest and cheapest wins in GenAI engineering live.** Most teams accept a 10–20× penalty because the naive path works. Today is the machinery that closes that gap. ##### Prefill and decode The single most important distinction in LLM serving. Generation has two phases with completely different performance characteristics. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph P["PREFILL — process the prompt"] P1["All prompt tokens
at once"] --> P2["Parallel attention
over full sequence"] P2 --> P3["KV cache populated"] P3 --> P4["First output token"] end subgraph D["DECODE — generate the rest"] D1["One token in"] --> D2["Attend to entire
KV cache"] D2 --> D3["One token out"] D3 --> D1 end P4 --> D1 P5["COMPUTE-bound
high GPU utilisation"] -.-> P D4["MEMORY-BANDWIDTH-bound
low GPU utilisation"] -.-> D ``` | | Prefill | Decode | |---|---|---| | Tokens processed | All prompt tokens in parallel | One at a time | | Bottleneck | **Compute** (matmul FLOPs) | **Memory bandwidth** (reading weights + KV cache) | | GPU utilisation | 60–80% | **5–15%** | | Scales with | Prompt length | Output length | | Metric | Time to first token (TTFT) | Time per output token (TPOT) | **Decode is why naive serving is so slow.** Generating one token requires reading the entire model — 16 GB for an 8B model in bf16 — plus the KV cache, from HBM. That is roughly 8ms of pure memory traffic at 2 TB/s, during which the tensor cores are almost idle. The insight that fixes it: **if you are reading the weights anyway, process many sequences at once.** Batch size 32 reads the weights once and produces 32 tokens. The memory traffic is nearly identical; throughput is 32×. ```python def decode_arithmetic(model_gb=16, kv_cache_gb_per_seq=0.5, hbm_tbps=2.0, batch_sizes=(1, 8, 32, 128)): """Why batching transforms decode throughput.""" for b in batch_sizes: bytes_read = (model_gb + kv_cache_gb_per_seq * b) * 1e9 seconds = bytes_read / (hbm_tbps * 1e12) print(f"batch {b:>4}: {seconds*1000:>6.2f} ms/step, " f"{b/seconds:>8.0f} tokens/s") # batch 1: 8.25 ms/step, 121 tokens/s # batch 8: 10.00 ms/step, 800 tokens/s # batch 32: 16.00 ms/step, 2000 tokens/s # batch 128: 40.00 ms/step, 3200 tokens/s ``` Batch 32 gives 16× the throughput for 2× the per-step latency. That trade is the foundation of every serving optimisation below. ##### PagedAttention The problem naive batching hits: **KV cache memory must be pre-allocated**, and you do not know how long a response will be. Traditional serving reserves `max_seq_len` per request. If your limit is 4,096 tokens and the average response is 200, you waste 95% of the allocation. Kwon et al. (2023) measured 60–80% waste in real systems. **PagedAttention borrows from operating-system virtual memory.** Split the KV cache into fixed-size blocks (typically 16 tokens), allocate blocks on demand, and maintain a block table mapping logical positions to physical blocks. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph N["Naive: contiguous pre-allocation"] N1["Req A: [used 200 |·········· wasted 3896 ··········]"] N2["Req B: [used 450 |········· wasted 3646 ··········]"] N3["Req C: [used 80 |··········· wasted 4016 ·········]"] end subgraph P["PagedAttention: block table"] P1["Req A → blocks [3, 7, 12]"] P2["Req B → blocks [1, 4, 8, 9, 15]"] P3["Req C → blocks [2, 5]"] P4["Free pool: [0, 6, 10, 11, 13, 14, ...]"] end N -.->|"~70% wasted"| X["fits ~8 concurrent"] P -.->|"<4% wasted"| Y["fits ~60 concurrent"] ``` ```python def kv_memory_comparison(max_seq=4096, avg_seq=350, n_layers=32, n_kv_heads=8, head_dim=128, dtype_bytes=2, gpu_kv_budget_gb=45): """How many concurrent sequences fit, naive versus paged?""" per_token = 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes naive_per_seq = per_token * max_seq paged_per_seq = per_token * avg_seq * 1.04 # ~4% block fragmentation return { "kv_bytes_per_token": per_token, "naive_concurrent": int(gpu_kv_budget_gb * 1e9 / naive_per_seq), "paged_concurrent": int(gpu_kv_budget_gb * 1e9 / paged_per_seq), "improvement": round(naive_per_seq / paged_per_seq, 1), } print(kv_memory_comparison()) # {'kv_bytes_per_token': 131072, 'naive_concurrent': 83, # 'paged_concurrent': 942, 'improvement': 11.3} ``` **Blocks also enable sharing.** Two requests with the same system prompt share the same physical blocks with copy-on-write semantics — which is prefix caching, covered on Day 32. ##### Continuous batching The second half of the vLLM gain, and the one people underestimate. **Static batching** collects N requests, runs them together, and returns when all finish. A request generating 30 tokens waits for one generating 800. **Continuous batching** (also called in-flight batching) operates at the iteration level: after every decode step, finished sequences leave the batch and queued requests join it. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph S["Static batching"] S1["t=0: [A,B,C,D] start"] --> S2["t=30: A done, slot IDLE"] S2 --> S3["t=45: C done, slot IDLE"] S3 --> S4["t=800: D done — batch returns"] S5["2 of 4 slots idle
for most of the run"] -.-> S4 end subgraph C["Continuous batching"] C1["t=0: [A,B,C,D]"] --> C2["t=30: A done → E joins"] C2 --> C3["t=45: C done → F joins"] C3 --> C4["t=60: E done → G joins"] C5["Batch stays full"] -.-> C4 end ``` ```python def batching_utilisation(output_lengths, batch_size=8): """Slot utilisation under static versus continuous batching.""" import numpy as np lengths = np.array(output_lengths) n_batches = int(np.ceil(len(lengths) / batch_size)) static_steps = sum( lengths[i * batch_size:(i + 1) * batch_size].max() for i in range(n_batches)) static_slots = static_steps * batch_size continuous_steps = lengths.sum() / batch_size return { "total_tokens": int(lengths.sum()), "static_slot_steps": int(static_slots), "static_utilisation": round(lengths.sum() / static_slots, 3), "continuous_utilisation": ">0.95 typically", "speedup": round(static_steps / continuous_steps, 2), } rng = np.random.default_rng(0) print(batching_utilisation(rng.lognormal(5.0, 1.0, 200).astype(int))) ``` **Real traffic has highly variable output lengths**, which is exactly the condition under which static batching wastes the most. Lognormal output distributions — short answers plus a long tail — are typical, and they are the worst case for static batching. ##### Serving with vLLM ```python from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams llm = LLM( model="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct", dtype="bfloat16", gpu_memory_utilization=0.90, # fraction of VRAM for weights + KV cache max_model_len=8192, enable_prefix_caching=True, tensor_parallel_size=1, max_num_seqs=256, # max concurrent sequences max_num_batched_tokens=8192, # prefill batching budget swap_space=4, # GB of CPU swap for preemption ) params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, max_tokens=512, stop=[""]) outputs = llm.generate(prompts, params) # batched automatically ``` **As an OpenAI-compatible server**, which is what you actually deploy: ```bash python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \ --model meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \ --max-model-len 8192 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --max-num-seqs 256 \ --tensor-parallel-size 1 \ --served-model-name llama3-8b \ --port 8000 ``` ```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="not-needed") response = client.chat.completions.create( model="llama3-8b", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain PagedAttention briefly."}], temperature=0.7, max_tokens=300, stream=True, ) ``` **The OpenAI-compatible interface is what makes this a drop-in change** — the Day 31 client code from the beginner track works unmodified against a self-hosted endpoint. **The parameters that matter most:** | Parameter | Effect | Guidance | |---|---|---| | `gpu_memory_utilization` | Fraction of VRAM used | 0.85–0.92; higher risks OOM under load | | `max_model_len` | Context limit | Set to your real maximum, not the model's | | `max_num_seqs` | Concurrency cap | 128–256; higher increases per-request latency | | `max_num_batched_tokens` | Prefill budget per step | 4096–16384; higher favours throughput | | `enable_prefix_caching` | Reuse shared prefixes | **Always on** for RAG or fixed system prompts | **`max_model_len` is the setting people leave too high.** Setting it to 32768 when your requests never exceed 4096 reserves KV cache headroom you never use and reduces achievable concurrency. ##### Text Generation Inference Hugging Face's TGI is the main alternative, with similar techniques and different operational characteristics. ```bash docker run --gpus all --shm-size 1g -p 8080:80 \ -v $PWD/data:/data \ ghcr.io/huggingface/text-generation-inference:latest \ --model-id meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-input-length 4096 \ --max-total-tokens 8192 \ --max-batch-prefill-tokens 8192 \ --quantize awq ``` | | vLLM | TGI | SGLang | TensorRT-LLM | |---|---|---|---|---| | PagedAttention | **Yes (origin)** | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Continuous batching | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Prefix caching | **Excellent** | Yes | **RadixAttention** | Yes | | Speculative decoding | Yes | Yes | Yes | **Yes, mature** | | LoRA hot-swap | **Yes, multi-adapter** | Yes | Yes | Limited | | Peak throughput | High | High | **Highest on structured** | **Highest raw** | | Setup effort | Low | **Lowest (Docker)** | Low | **High (compilation)** | | Hardware | NVIDIA, AMD | NVIDIA, AMD, Inferentia | NVIDIA | NVIDIA only | **Practical guidance:** vLLM as the default — largest community, best documentation, strong multi-LoRA support. TGI if you want a Docker-first deployment with minimal Python. SGLang if your workload has heavy prefix sharing (agents, RAG with a fixed system prompt). TensorRT-LLM when you need maximum throughput on NVIDIA and can absorb the compilation complexity. ##### Throughput versus latency These trade against each other, and the right point depends entirely on your product. ```python from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class ServingProfile: name: str max_num_seqs: int max_num_batched_tokens: int scheduling: str rationale: str PROFILES = { "interactive_chat": ServingProfile( "interactive_chat", max_num_seqs=64, max_num_batched_tokens=4096, scheduling="prioritise decode", rationale="TTFT under 500ms matters more than aggregate throughput"), "batch_processing": ServingProfile( "batch_processing", max_num_seqs=256, max_num_batched_tokens=32768, scheduling="prioritise prefill", rationale="no user waiting; maximise tokens per rupee"), "balanced_api": ServingProfile( "balanced_api", max_num_seqs=128, max_num_batched_tokens=8192, scheduling="chunked prefill", rationale="bounded TTFT with good throughput"), } ``` **Chunked prefill** is the technique that reconciles them. A long prompt's prefill is split into chunks and interleaved with decode steps for other requests, so one 8,000-token prompt does not stall every in-flight generation. ```bash --enable-chunked-prefill --max-num-batched-tokens 2048 ``` Without it, a single long-context request causes a visible latency spike for every concurrent user — a common and confusing production symptom. **The metrics to track:** | Metric | Definition | Matters for | |---|---|---| | **TTFT** | Time to first token | Perceived responsiveness | | **TPOT** | Time per output token after the first | Streaming smoothness | | **E2E latency** | TTFT + TPOT × output length | Total wait | | **Throughput** | Output tokens/second across all requests | Cost per token | | **Goodput** | Requests/second meeting the SLA | **The real number** | **Goodput is the metric that should drive tuning.** Throughput of 3,000 tokens/second means nothing if half your requests exceed a 2-second TTFT budget. ##### Benchmarking ```python import asyncio import time import numpy as np from openai import AsyncOpenAI async def benchmark_serving(base_url, model, prompts, concurrency=32, max_tokens=256, ttft_sla_s=1.0): """Measure TTFT, TPOT, throughput, and goodput under concurrent load.""" client = AsyncOpenAI(base_url=base_url, api_key="none") sem = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency) records = [] async def one(prompt): async with sem: t0 = time.perf_counter() ttft = None n_tokens = 0 stream = await client.chat.completions.create( model=model, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], max_tokens=max_tokens, temperature=0.7, stream=True, ) async for chunk in stream: if chunk.choices and chunk.choices[0].delta.content: if ttft is None: ttft = time.perf_counter() - t0 n_tokens += 1 total = time.perf_counter() - t0 records.append({ "ttft": ttft or total, "e2e": total, "tokens": n_tokens, "tpot": (total - (ttft or 0)) / max(n_tokens - 1, 1), }) wall_start = time.perf_counter() await asyncio.gather(*[one(p) for p in prompts]) wall = time.perf_counter() - wall_start ttfts = np.array([r["ttft"] for r in records]) tpots = np.array([r["tpot"] for r in records]) total_tokens = sum(r["tokens"] for r in records) return { "concurrency": concurrency, "requests": len(records), "wall_s": round(wall, 2), "throughput_tok_s": round(total_tokens / wall, 1), "requests_per_s": round(len(records) / wall, 2), "ttft_p50_ms": round(float(np.percentile(ttfts, 50)) * 1000, 1), "ttft_p95_ms": round(float(np.percentile(ttfts, 95)) * 1000, 1), "tpot_p50_ms": round(float(np.percentile(tpots, 50)) * 1000, 2), "goodput_rps": round( float((ttfts <= ttft_sla_s).sum()) / wall, 2), } async def sweep_concurrency(base_url, model, prompts, levels=(1, 8, 32, 64, 128)): results = [] for c in levels: r = await benchmark_serving(base_url, model, prompts, concurrency=c) results.append(r) print(f"c={c:>4}: {r['throughput_tok_s']:>7.0f} tok/s, " f"TTFT p95 {r['ttft_p95_ms']:>7.1f}ms, " f"goodput {r['goodput_rps']:>5.2f} rps") return results ``` A representative sweep for Llama-3-8B on one A100: | Concurrency | throughput tok/s | TTFT p50 | TTFT p95 | goodput rps | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 118 | 42ms | 61ms | 0.46 | | 8 | 782 | 89ms | 148ms | 3.1 | | 32 | 2,410 | 214ms | 512ms | 9.4 | | **64** | **3,180** | 398ms | 947ms | **12.4** | | 128 | 3,520 | 812ms | **2,140ms** | 8.1 | **Goodput peaks at concurrency 64 and drops at 128**, even though raw throughput keeps rising — because p95 TTFT crosses the 1-second SLA and those requests no longer count. That inflection is the number you tune to, and you cannot see it from throughput alone. ##### Tensor parallelism for serving When the model does not fit on one GPU, or when you need lower latency than one GPU can deliver. ```bash python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \ --model meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 ``` Day 9's tensor parallelism, applied to inference: weight matrices are sharded across GPUs, with an all-reduce per transformer block. **Set TP degree to the number of GPUs in one node**, because the all-reduce traffic requires NVLink. TP across nodes over Ethernet is dramatically slower. **TP must divide the attention heads evenly.** A model with 32 heads supports TP of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, or 32 — not 3 or 6. **Diminishing returns are real:** ```python def tp_efficiency(base_throughput=3180, tp_degrees=(1, 2, 4, 8), comm_overhead=0.12): """Communication overhead grows with TP degree.""" for tp in tp_degrees: ideal = base_throughput * tp actual = ideal * (1 - comm_overhead) ** (tp - 1).bit_length() print(f"TP={tp}: {actual:>7.0f} tok/s, efficiency {actual/ideal:.0%}") ``` **Pipeline parallelism** across nodes is the option when a model exceeds one node, but it adds a bubble and is generally worse for latency than TP. Prefer a quantized model on fewer GPUs if quality allows — Day 33's material. ##### Common mistakes - **Naive `generate()` in a request handler** — the 18× penalty. - **`max_model_len` far above your real maximum**, wasting KV cache headroom. - **`gpu_memory_utilization` at 0.99**, causing OOM under load spikes. - **No chunked prefill**, so one long prompt stalls every concurrent request. - **Prefix caching disabled** with a long fixed system prompt. - **Tuning for throughput and ignoring goodput** — high throughput with SLA violations is not useful. - **Reporting mean latency** instead of TTFT p95. - **TP degree that does not divide the head count.** - **TP across nodes** without high-speed interconnect. - **Benchmarking with uniform prompt and output lengths**, which hides the variability that continuous batching exists to handle. - **No warm-up** before measuring — the first requests include CUDA graph capture and weight loading. ##### Hands-on: measure the gap yourself Your practical task serves a model with vLLM and benchmarks it against a naive Hugging Face `generate()` loop. Use realistic prompt and output length distributions — lognormal output lengths, not fixed 100 tokens — because uniform lengths make static batching look far better than it is. Expect somewhere between 8× and 20× depending on your variability, and note which of the three mechanisms contributed most. The mini project deploys an OpenAI-compatible vLLM endpoint and load-tests it, tuning for throughput. **Sweep concurrency and plot goodput, not throughput.** Find the inflection point where TTFT p95 crosses your SLA, and set `max_num_seqs` just below it. Then enable chunked prefill and re-run with a few long prompts mixed in — the improvement in tail latency is usually dramatic. The assignment explains why PagedAttention and continuous batching improve throughput, with measured results. Include the memory arithmetic showing how many concurrent sequences fit under each scheme, and the slot-utilisation calculation for static versus continuous batching on your own output-length distribution. Numbers from your own benchmark are what make the explanation credible. ##### Key takeaways - **Prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bandwidth-bound** — decode leaves the GPU 85–95% idle, which is why batching transforms throughput. - **PagedAttention eliminates KV cache waste** by allocating fixed-size blocks on demand, typically increasing concurrency by an order of magnitude. - **Continuous batching keeps the batch full** by admitting new requests at every decode step, which matters most when output lengths vary — as real traffic always does. - **Tune for goodput, not throughput.** Raw tokens per second keeps rising past the point where p95 TTFT violates your SLA and requests stop counting. - **Enable chunked prefill and prefix caching**, set `max_model_len` to your real maximum, and keep tensor parallelism within a single NVLink node.
practical_task_reference: Serve a model with vLLM and benchmark throughput and latency against a naive Hugging Face generate loop.
mini_project_reference: Deploy an OpenAI-compatible vLLM endpoint and load-test it, tuning batch and concurrency for best throughput.
assignment_reference: Write an explainer on why PagedAttention and continuous batching improve throughput, with measured results.
